skyline.text: Amit Varma on why fret­ting about low-value tourists isn’t snob­bery
How high-value tourists kept mov­ing on, and why cricket is next
Freedom first, mar­ket fail­ure next, and only then the state

masthead.footnote: *It will take hundred years to become Switzerland. Page 2

brief.head: Tourists who fly
brief.text: Kangra’s run­way is about 1,300 me­tres, Ajay Shah thinks, and Kullu’s about 1,100: too short for big air­craft. High-value tourists fly, so Himachal needs longer run­ways. {058-C10}

brief.head: When hardware sells
brief.text: Malini Goyal says Bangalore’s soft­ware is 5G but its hard­ware 2G. In Bir, Amit Varma said, the soft­ware is the hard­ware, and it must be made 5G. {058-J11}

brief.head: What’s in a name?
brief.text: By a lake in Udaipur[[x1]], a year be­fore launch, Amit Varma re­called, the hosts came up with two names: *Watching the Wheels* and *Everything is Everything*[[x2]]. {058-J10}

brief.head: Knobs for regions
brief.text: Steven Pinker’s line that na­ture gives us knobs[[x3]][[x4]] and nur­ture turns them ap­plies to re­gions too, Amit Varma sug­gested: each place has dif­fer­ent knobs, so pol­icy must fit. {058-J07}

brief.head: A reserve for two
brief.text: Ideally, Ajay Shah said, India and Nepal would run the Kangchenjunga re­serve to­gether. Sikkim’s part cov­ers 2,000 of the state’s roughly 7,000 square kilo­me­tres, and Nepal holds an­other 2,000. {#sikkim}

thought.who: Ajay Shah, making the case that the hills should build on what no one else has

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on tourism in the Himalayas
lead.head: Selling the view without losing it

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 58

body: The last of ten episodes recorded in a week at Bir, in Himachal Pradesh, grew out of a meet­ing with a viewer. Shubham Dhiman drove three hours from his vil­lage near Hamirpur to meet Amit Varma and Ajay Shah, and told them what he wanted.
“I don’t want to go and work in a city, I want to do some­thing for Himachal,” Varma re­called him say­ing. {058-S01}
In Dhiman’s con­ver­sa­tion with Shah, the ques­tion came up that this episode takes on: how can places like this de­velop with­out de­stroy­ing what is al­ready there?
Shah set the terms at once. The goal is sus­tained eco­nomic growth for the peo­ple of the Himalayan states, not scenery for out­siders.

“Sometimes there is an outsider’s con­de­scend­ing view that we want you to live at low lev­els of in­come be­cause we would like your places to be nice for us,” he said. “And I’m not there at all.” {058-C01}
## Only one Himalayas

The plains recipe of fac­to­ries, high­ways and mod­ern farm­ing would not work, Shah ar­gued. The hill states are land­locked, far from the con­tainer ships, and moun­tain in­fra­struc­ture is so costly that they would al­ways do it worse than the plains.

Better to build on what no one else has. Switzerland and Colorado sell their beau­ti­ful lo­cales, and their peo­ple have stayed pros­per­ous for gen­er­a­tions. “The glory of the Himalayan states is the Himalayas,” he said. {058-C03}
Udaipur had shown the way, he said, when Rajasthan gave its lakes first claim on scarce water, ahead of farm­ing.
The peo­ple are not the ob­sta­cle once feared. Fertility is low across the hills and peo­ple are leav­ing them, Shah said, so the old worry about crowds clear­ing the forests is out of date.
## Where it goes wrong

Left alone, Shah said, every hotel and restau­rant adds disco lights, loud­speak­ers and bon­fires to pull in cus­tomers, and spoils the area around it. “They’ve just de­stroyed a cir­cle with a ra­dius of two hun­dred me­tres sur­round­ing them­selves.” {058-C06}
Tourism in­come is the num­ber of tourists times what each spends. Chase the num­bers and the big spenders go.

Dharamshala, near Bir, showed the re­sult. Each step up the hill, from Dharamshala to McLeod Ganj to Dharamkot, en­joyed a good 20 or 30 years and then de­cayed into what Shah called “a sta­ble equi­lib­rium of poverty”.
Varma in­sisted that wor­ry­ing about low-value tourists was not snob­bery. In that equi­lib­rium, he said, the lo­cals earn less and the beauty is de­stroyed: “a lose-lose game”.
## Bir be­fore Bangalore
Shah’s reme­dies were town plan­ning and urban gov­er­nance: lines on maps for streets and parks be­fore build­ing swal­lows the land, and a state that fines who­ever lights a fire.

Small Bir, he ar­gued, is a bet­ter bet than big Bangalore. Bangalore sells soft­ware, so its res­i­dents put up with a bro­ken city. Bir sells it­self. “So in Bangalore, peo­ple are much more ca­sual about lit­ter­ing be­cause their busi­ness is soft­ware.” {058-C09}
Parks, too, could earn far more, as America’s Yellowstone does.
None of it is quick, Shah warned. But the dream, he said, should be that Bir can be­come the Switzerland of India.

second.label: Rajasthan’s big bet
second.head: The lakes jump the queue
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how Rajasthan put tourism ahead of farming in Udaipur

pic.caption: The City Palace in Udaipur, Rajasthan, seen across the water in 2018

body: Udaipur’s lakes used to de­pend on the mon­soon, Ajay Shah said. In a good year the city was stag­ger­ingly beau­ti­ful. In oth­ers the water evap­o­rated, and peo­ple would check with each other that “the lakes are nice” be­fore going.

Then Vasundhara Raje, Rajiv Mehrishi and oth­ers changed Rajasthan’s rules for ir­ri­ga­tion water: what­ever the scarcity, Udaipur’s lakes would come first. Farmers lower in the queue lost out in the short term. {058-S02}

Shah called it a triv­ial cal­cu­la­tion. Rajasthan is not a great place for agri­cul­ture, and Udaipur, “the Venice of the East”, now makes se­ri­ous money from high-value tourism, with lakhs of peo­ple tied to its econ­omy. {058-J12}

quote.text: Whatever be the scarcity of water, first, Udaipur lakes will get water.

third.head: Parks that pay their way

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the parks that could earn

body: Indian na­tional parks do two things well, Ajay Shah said: they stop poach­ing and they stop com­mer­cial de­vel­op­ment. What they have not done is earn. “We’ve not yet fig­ured out how to con­trib­ute to the GDP.” {058-C11}

His head­line was Yellowstone, in the United States. It gets four mil­lion tourists a year, he said, each spend­ing be­tween $1,000 and $2,000: four to eight bil­lion dol­lars of rev­enue. {#yellowstone}

His model for the Great Himalayan National Park: beau­ti­ful gate­way vil­lages like Bir on its edge, hun­dreds of kilo­me­tres of walk­ing trails in­side, camp­grounds, and a lit­tle high-end lodg­ing run by pri­vate op­er­a­tors bound by strict bio­di­ver­sity clauses.
Protecting wildlife and be­com­ing a Switzerland, Shah said, can go to­gether. “These goals are not in­con­sis­tent.”

quote.text: The air­ports, the high­ways, the rail­way lines in these states will al­ways be 50% in­fe­rior to what is done in the plains.

box.title: The meetup behind the episode
box.text: At a viewers’ meetup in Bir, Shubham Dhiman, who had driven three hours from a vil­lage near Hamirpur and done Takshashila’s pub­lic pol­icy course, talked pol­icy with Ajay Shah. Amit Varma’s first thought, he ad­mit­ted, was “episode”. {058-J02}

sections.label: The strategy
sections.head: Not a hill-top Haryana
sections.caption: the plains recipe and the Himalayas
body: Ajay Shah calls him­self an eco­nomic growth fun­da­men­tal­ist. So he framed the ques­tion as the path to sus­tained growth for the peo­ple of the Himalayan states, from Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh to Nepal, Bhutan and the North East. His only loy­alty, he said, is to their wel­fare and liveli­hoods. {058-C01}

Amit Varma asked whether re­gions, like peo­ple, come with knobs[[x6]] of dif­fer­ent sizes. Shah’s an­swer was the sub­sidiar­ity prin­ci­ple[[x5]]: the local po­lit­i­cal sys­tem should set its own pri­or­i­ties.

Haryana, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat have a stan­dard recipe: build in­fra­struc­ture, at­tract big fac­to­ries, raise farm yields. It does not travel up­hill. The Himalayan states are land­locked and will never have the coast­line that opens up trade by con­tainer ship. Mountain air­ports, rail­ways and high­ways cost so much that user charges would be very high.
## The asset no­body else has
Follow the plains recipe, Shah said, and “in a way you’re a bit doomed”, al­ways doing it im­per­fectly, with a per capita GDP much worse than in the plains. {058-C02}
The al­ter­na­tive is to build on what no­body can copy. Switzerland and Colorado sell their beau­ti­ful lo­cales, and tourism there is among the world’s most pros­per­ous in­dus­tries. {058-C03}
~ “Udaipur has its lakes and the Himalayan states have the Himalayas,” Shah said. The harder ques­tion was how to make that last.

quote.text: The air­ports, the high­ways, the rail­way lines in these states will al­ways be 50% in­fe­rior to what is done in the plains.

sections.label: The people
sections.head: Fewer hands, empty homes
sections.caption: the hills’ demographic turn
body: Amit Varma turned from the place to its peo­ple. Two ar­gu­ments, Ajay Shah said, could once have sunk a tourism strat­egy: too many work­ers for an in­dus­try that uses few, and so many peo­ple that forests would be cleared for farms and houses.

Those prob­lems are largely be­hind us, he said. The total fer­til­ity rate in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand is around 1.6 and 1.7, sim­i­lar in Sikkim and Bhutan. Rapid pop­u­la­tion growth is a thing of the past. {058-C04}
Low birth rates and mi­gra­tion out of the hills mean pro­jec­tions of a gen­tle de­cline in the pop­u­la­tion and in the work­ing-age pop­u­la­tion.
## Villages with­out peo­ple
In Uttarakhand there are more than 3,000 aban­doned vil­lages, Shah said, and he has hiked through them. {#villages} He has started to see the same in the deep Sahyadris.
Leaving is ra­tio­nal, he said. In the re­mote moun­tains a good life is hard to sus­tain, and peo­ple want to be nearer the cities.
~ The fear of hu­mans clear­ing forests be­longed to 1950 and 1960, Shah said. “But that’s not where we are today.”

quote.text: So the age of rapid pop­u­la­tion growth is over, in fact.

sections.label: The drift
sections.head: The 200-metre circle
sections.caption: the bonfire next door
body: What hap­pens if no­body does any­thing? Amit Varma asked. Ajay Shah said the ques­tion ap­plied the recipe of pub­lic eco­nom­ics[[x7]]: start from free­dom and re­spect people’s cre­ativ­ity, find what goes wrong, and only then “start like John Maynard Keynes and won­der” whether the state can add value. {058-C05}

The story he told be­gins with one beau­ti­ful vil­lage, barely dis­cov­ered. Word spreads like wild­fire: first come the Instagrammers, then the YouTubers. {#instagram} Every local, in ra­tio­nal self-interest, wants to make money from it. Shacks and houses go up; then come traf­fic jams, disco lights and loud­speak­ers play­ing all night.
## A mar­ket fail­ure hid­ing in­side

Hiding in­side this, Shah said, is a mar­ket fail­ure: the neg­a­tive ex­ter­nal­ity. A pizza place that in­stalls glitzy disco lights and five thou­sand watts of am­pli­fi­ca­tion thinks it is at­tract­ing tourists. In fact it has made a 200-metre zone around it­self where no­body wants to go. {058-C06}
Let N be the num­ber of tourists and P what each spends per day. A region’s tourism in­come is N times P. Maximise N, he said, and P falls: the high-value tourists stop com­ing.

~ Shah’s pic­ture of an un­man­aged Bir: five restau­rants com­pet­ing with “five thou­sand watts and ten thou­sand watts” and lights “blink­ing so that the aliens can see us from Alpha Centauri”. {058-J03}

quote.text: Start at the base­line, free­dom is nor­mal, peo­ple will do what­ever they want.

sections.label: The trap
sections.head: Boom, bust, repeat
sections.caption: the low-income trap
body: Amit Varma said Ajay Shah’s fore­cast for Bir was not the­ory but prac­tice: it had al­ready hap­pened, in the neigh­bour­hood, in Dharamshala.

Shah de­scribed the pat­tern. A place gets twenty or thirty good years. Then it falls into a sta­ble equi­lib­rium of poverty, held there by low-value tourists, who do not need high human cap­i­tal to serve them and who dam­age the place fur­ther. {058-C07}

Building human cap­i­tal, he said, is a hun­dred-year jour­ney. Sustainability means an arc of in­come that keeps ris­ing over that span, as in Switzerland, Colorado and Japan, where peo­ple have gone back for gen­er­a­tions.
## Not snob­bery

Varma an­tic­i­pated a charge. Talk of low-value tourists, he said, “sounds re­ally snob­bish”. But nei­ther his view nor the visitors’ was the point. What mat­tered was how the local peo­ple and the local econ­omy were doing.

A low-level equi­lib­rium, he said, “al­most seems like a lose-lose game”: lo­cals make less money than they oth­er­wise would, and ev­ery­thing beau­ti­ful about the place is grad­u­ally de­stroyed. {#loselose}
~ There are no quick fixes, Shah said, and no sil­ver bul­lets. “It will take hun­dred years to be­come Switzerland.” But if things are done right, he said, the pos­si­bil­ity is there. {#hundred}

quote.text: You get brief growth, it goes away. You get brief growth, it goes away.

sections.label: The toolkit
sections.head: Draw the streets first
sections.caption: lines on maps for Bir
body: What can be done? Ajay Shah’s an­swer came in two parts: town plan­ning and urban gov­er­nance, then parks. Much of what is known about cities, he said, car­ries straight over to the hills.

Bir has a land­ing zone for paraglid­ers but no other parks. Following Bimal Patel[[x8]], Shah would draw lines on maps now, set­ting aside 40 to 50 per cent of the land for streets and parks be­fore un­planned build­ing makes that im­pos­si­ble. {058-C08}

Across the road from the land­ing ground he imag­ined cafés and no ve­hi­cles, like the walk­ing cen­tre of a Swiss town. “So it be­comes a walk­ing zone where it can just be so beau­ti­ful.” {#walking}
## Who lit that fire?
Then pub­lic goods, such as clean air. Fires around Bir fill the air with smoke, and Shah would fine who­ever lit one. {058-S05}

Amit Varma raised the ob­vi­ous worry: high mod­ernism, the top-down en­gi­neer­ing mind­set[[x9]], de­manded of an Indian state with low ca­pa­bil­ity. {#modernism} Perhaps basic rule of law was the safer de­fault.

~ Shah wanted rule of law too, but said urban mar­ket fail­ures call for more. He re­jects Indian-style plan­ning that spec­i­fies every school and petrol pump. There is no run­ning away from town plan­ning, he said.

quote.text: You are stuck if you don’t have that forty, fifty per­cent of the land al­lo­cated to the streets and the parks.

sections.label: The proof
sections.head: Small town, better odds
sections.caption: why Bir beats Bangalore
body: Amit Varma agreed with all of it, and then wor­ried about iso­mor­phic mimicry[[x10]]: tak­ing a vi­sion of town plan­ning and ask­ing an Indian state to de­liver it with­out the ca­pa­bil­ity or the pol­i­tics to do so. {#mimicry} Were there ex­am­ples closer to home?
Ajay Shah named com­mu­nity suc­cesses he knew of in Meghalaya, Bhutan and Nepal, where peo­ple un­der­stood the down­hill slide and came to­gether.

But knowl­edge comes first, he said. Anyone try­ing to act on this should reach past nor­mal Indian town plan­ning to ex­perts at the fron­tier, such as Bimal Patel, and draw on urban-governance hands such as Pritika Hingorani.

Bir is also a smaller prob­lem. “You must learn to walk be­fore you can run,” he said, a chap­ter title from *In Service of the Republic*, which he wrote with Vijay Kelkar. Reformers should learn in small towns first. {058-J13}
## Selling the place it­self

And the in­cen­tives line up. Bangalore sells soft­ware, so res­i­dents grum­ble but put up with a bro­ken city, while a preda­tory state ex­tracts money from the soft­ware mak­ers. Bir sells the place it­self. {058-C09}
~ Udaipur shows the ef­fect, Shah said. Its po­lice treat a woman’s safety on the streets at 2 AM as make or break, be­cause one bad event can cost the town mil­lions of dol­lars. {#twoam}

quote.text: Whereas in Bir, what you’re sell­ing is a beau­ti­ful vil­lage, is a beau­ti­ful town.

So this is how the Great Himalayan National Park can si­mul­ta­ne­ously serve the re­quire­ments of wildlife pro­tec­tion and bio­di­ver­sity pro­tec­tion, but also cater to the goals of be­com­ing a Switzerland and hav­ing a high per capita GDP.

p3.title: Tales from the hills
p3.deck: Four tales from the Himalayas and the Sahyadris, and what each one teaches

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the hill town that taught him the problem
stories.head: Going downhill, moving uphill
body: For Ajay Shah, Dharamshala was an aha mo­ment: the place where he un­der­stood how a hill town goes bad, and how the dam­age climbs up­hill. Amit Varma had asked about it be­cause it is lit­er­ally in Bir’s neigh­bour­hood.
The story be­gins with the Dalai Lama in 1959. The air­port came, Shah thinks, in 1960 or so, and Dharamshala was great. {#dalai}

There was no Instagram then and there were no YouTubers, so the memo took time to get out. Fame spread qui­etly, by word of mouth and through the *Lonely Planet*, and more and more peo­ple started com­ing.
By the eight­ies, he said, Dharamshala was over­crowded. “It be­came a bad Indian city,” with all the prob­lems of urban gov­er­nance, and the high-value tourists moved up to McLeod Ganj.

McLeod Ganj worked for about twenty years be­fore it, too, started going bad. The high-value tourists moved to Lower Dharamkot. When the bad things started hap­pen­ing there, they moved on to Upper Dharamkot.

Then came what Shah called “a very bad event”: Dharamshala’s rise as a cricket sta­dium. “And cricket un­for­tu­nately goes with very low value tourists,” he said. His pre­dic­tion is that Upper Dharamkot will rapidly be de­stroyed. {058-S04}

~ Each place, he said, had its pe­riod of high value, ris­ing prop­erty prices and human cap­i­tal being built. Then the neg­a­tive ex­ter­nal­i­ties kicked in, and it sank back into low-value tourism and a sta­ble equi­lib­rium of poverty.
stories.why: Without urban gov­er­nance, de­cline comes as a stair­case: a 20- or 30-year bloom, ruin by neg­a­tive ex­ter­nal­i­ties, then the high-value vis­i­tors move fur­ther up­hill. Each step leaves a town locked in low-value tourism.
stories.postscript: When Shah later blamed “the cricket peo­ple” again, Varma apol­o­gised: “we love cricket. All cricket peo­ple are not the same, we con­tain mul­ti­tudes.” {058-J04}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Dharamshala’s slide uphill

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s hikes through India’s abandoned villages
stories.head: Two hundred houses, three families
body: On the way up to Panchachuli[[x11]], Ajay Shah stayed in a vil­lage of about 200 houses where three fam­i­lies still lived. Each hiker was of­fered an en­tire house for the night. {058-S03}
On the Pindari Glacier trek he heard men talk of a preg­nant woman whom four men had to carry on a stretcher for 20 kilo­me­tres to reach the near­est health­care fa­cil­ity. {#stretcher}
Uttarakhand has more than 3,000 such vil­lages, he said. In the re­mote moun­tains a good life is hard to sus­tain, and mov­ing to the city is ra­tio­nal.

~ Now he sees it in the deep Sahyadris too. On a nine-day trek in January, the one on which he broke his ankle[[x12]] on the fifth day, he reached a vil­lage on day three with about twenty houses, one old man and one old woman. {#sahyadri}

quote.text: And there were three fam­i­lies liv­ing there. Meaning there were about 197 empty houses.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the abandoned villages

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a view lost in smoke, and how to clear it
stories.head: Where there’s smoke, send a drone
body: The day be­fore record­ing, the crew stood at Billing, 2,500 me­tres up, and looked down at Bir, 800 me­tres below. What they saw was a haze of solid par­tic­u­late mat­ter.
There were fires, Ajay Shah said, some per­haps lit by tourists with bon­fires, “re­ally the bad kinds of tourists”. From the land­ing ground below, you can barely see Billing.

Everybody’s view is dam­aged, he said, and the beauty of the whole place with it: a neg­a­tive ex­ter­nal­ity that no in­di­vid­ual can fix. {058-S05} “Only the state can fix air qual­ity in North India.”
~ His fix: put drones in the air[[x13]] to see every fire with ther­mal cam­eras, and send a po­lice­man to fine who­ever lit it ten thou­sand ru­pees. {#fine}
stories.why: Clean air and a clear view are pub­lic goods. A bon­fire pleases one hotel’s guests and harms ev­ery­one, which is where even a free­dom-first thinker says the state must act. {058-C05}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the haze over Bir

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the book that made him a hiker
stories.head: A book fair, then the Sahyadris
body: At about eleven, Ajay Shah walked into a book fair in Bombay and stum­bled on *Trek the Sahyadris* by Harish Kapadia, a moun­taineer and an en­thu­si­ast of the great out­doors in India. {#bookfair}
He bought it and read it a hun­dred times. Then, on his own, with no help and no knowl­edge, he and a bunch of other kids from Bandra East started hik­ing in the Sahyadris.
It was a turn­ing point in his life, he said. “So thank you, Harish Kapadia, you changed my life.” {058-S06}
~ Kapadia has a new book from 2023, *Autumn Passage to the Himalaya*, which Shah called one of the lovely books for any­one who takes an in­ter­est in the Himalayas. {058-R04}
stories.why: One book, found by chance at the right age, can shape a whole life. Amit Varma sug­gested Shah could now be that spark for young peo­ple, and urged view­ers to watch the hik­ing episode[[x14]].

quiz.q: What did Rajasthan change so that Udaipur’s lakes would no longer depend on a good monsoon?
quiz.a: The ir­ri­ga­tion rules: Udaipur’s lakes get water first, what­ever the scarcity, ahead of farm­ing.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, should Himachal Pradesh want longer airport runways?
quiz.a: High-value tourists fly; Kangra’s and Kullu’s short run­ways can­not take big air­craft.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah fear for Upper Dharamkot now that Dharamshala hosts cricket?
quiz.a: Cricket brings very low-value tourists, and he pre­dicts Upper Dharamkot will soon be de­stroyed.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s formula for tourism income, what are N and P, and what goes wrong?
quiz.a: Tourist num­bers and daily spend; chas­ing more tourists drives down what each one spends.

quiz.q: How would Ajay Shah stop the fires that fill Bir’s air with smoke?
quiz.a: Drones with ther­mal cam­eras to spot fires, and a ten-thousand-rupee fine for who­ever lit them.

quiz.q: Which book, found at a Bombay book fair at about eleven, made Ajay Shah a hiker?
quiz.a: Harish Kapadia’s *Trek the Sahyadris*, which he read a hun­dred times.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 58. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Udaipur (Gerd Eichmann, CC BY-SA 4.0); Vijay Kelkar (Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Open Library.

shelf.title: Order Without Design
shelf.creator: Alain Bertaud
shelf.why: Amit’s desert-island book on cities: Bertaud brings eco­nom­ics and many other dis­ci­plines to urban plan­ning, ex­poses the fol­lies of high mod­ernism and re­spects the local knowl­edge be­hind why streets and cities work as they do.

shelf.title: Horizon
shelf.creator: Barry Lopez
shelf.why: Lopez is one of the great travel writ­ers and a beau­ti­ful, in­tro­spec­tive writer.

shelf.title: Trek the Sahyadris
shelf.creator: Harish Kapadia
shelf.why: It was a turn­ing point in his life.

shelf.title: Autumn Passage to the Himalaya
shelf.creator: Harish Kapadia
shelf.why: Ajay calls it a lovely book and es­sen­tial if you take an in­ter­est in the Himalayas.

shelf.title: Unboxing Bengaluru
shelf.creator: Malini Goyal and Prashanth Prakash
shelf.why: A book on Bangalore with a line Amit loves: its soft­ware is 5G but its hard­ware 2G, a fail­ure of gov­er­nance.

shelf.title: Malini Goyal is the Curious One (Episode 377 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Journalist Malini Goyal on Bangalore: her di­ag­no­sis of a city with 5G soft­ware and 2G hard­ware, and her re­search on its dat­ing cul­ture, which found that when ev­ery­one has ten choices, peo­ple who want a part­ner to grow with strug­gle to find one.

shelf.title: Pritika Hingorani Wants to Fix Our Cities (Episode 361 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Background on the urban gov­er­nance knowl­edge that Ajay says can carry straight over to Himalayan towns.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Indian farm­ing, which em­ploys 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich coun­tries, is held back by the lack of a work­ing price sys­tem: MSPs that favour ce­re­als over pulses, loan waivers in­stead of struc­tural re­form, gluts and col­laps­ing prices.

shelf.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The ar­gu­ment that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs: hu­mans are in­no­va­tors whose cre­ativ­ity beats scarcity, so India’s prob­lem is too few chil­dren and too lit­tle train­ing of minds, not too many peo­ple.

shelf.title: The Hiking Episode (Episode 35)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay on his pas­sion for hik­ing, from the Goecha La trek be­neath Kanchenjunga to why the worst ac­ci­dents hap­pen when you think you’re al­most home.

shelf.title: Public Policy courses at Takshashila
shelf.creator: Takshashila Institution
shelf.why: Shubham, a pol­icy-curious young Himachali who in­spired the episode, came through this course.

laughs.text: Amit ad­mits that while lis­ten­ing to Ajay talk with Shubham, his first thought was ‘episode!’ Then he cor­rects him­self: the proper phrase is ‘knowl­edge to the world’, not talk of churn­ing out con­tent.
Ajay’s pic­ture of an un­man­aged Bir: five restau­rants com­pet­ing with ‘five thou­sand watts and ten thou­sand watts’ and lights ‘blink­ing so that the aliens can see us from Alpha Centauri.’

Amit, after Ajay’s jab at cricket crowds: ‘If there are any cricket peo­ple watch­ing this, kindly ex­cuse, we love you, I love you, we love cricket. All cricket peo­ple are not the same, we con­tain mul­ti­tudes.’
Ajay’s offer to view­ers: ‘if you ask us in trip­li­cate, we will give you the lat­i­tude and lon­gi­tude of the lo­ca­tion where each ses­sion was recorded.’
Amit stop­ping his own re­flec­tion on inner jour­neys: ‘...sound­ing like a pop philoso­pher. Enough of this.’
Dire Straits’ ‘Telegraph Road’ from Love Over Gold, the song Ajay thinks of as he de­scribes a pris­tine place being dis­cov­ered by Instagrammers and YouTubers and then built over.
Malini Goyal’s line on Bangalore: ‘the soft­ware is 5G, but the hard­ware is 2G.’ Amit adds that in Bir the soft­ware is the hard­ware and needs to be made 5G.
‘You must learn to walk be­fore you can run’, a chap­ter title from Kelkar and Shah’s In Service of the Republic, used to argue that urban re­form­ers should start with small towns.
